title: Tibo's pricing playbook: require a credit card, charge more, A/B test constantly
summary: Tibo explains why his small-team SaaS products require a credit card before a free trial, why a free tier must earn its keep as acquisition cost, and why bootstrapped B2B founders should charge $40-$100/month instead of $9. He also argues for constant one-metric-at-a-time A/B testing and for choosing a model that fits your own constraints.

principles.text: Require a credit card for trials: it filters for serious users and lifts trial-to-paid conversion, at the cost of volume.
principles.quote: Requiring a credit card creates commitment. If you're willing to enter your card, you're not just curious. You're serious about testing it.

principles.text: Prefer 100 serious trials over 1,000 sign-ups who ghost, especially when your team is tiny and can't absorb support load.
principles.quote: I'd rather have 100 serious trials than 1,000 people who sign up and ghost.

principles.text: Judge a free tier by the job it does: acquisition cost if it finds future buyers, charity if it only serves people who never pay.
principles.quote: The question isn't "should we have a free tier?" It's "what job is the free tier doing?"

principles.text: AI products carry real marginal costs, so free tiers must be deliberately limited and tracked against actual conversion data.
principles.quote: Does your free tier bring you people who eventually pay, or just people looking for free stuff?

principles.text: Small teams and indie hackers should charge more, not less. Fewer customers at $99 beat many at $9 and free time to improve the product.
principles.quote: More indie hackers and small teams should make their apps fully paid and charge MORE, not less.

principles.text: A higher price forces higher quality and gives a clean ROI signal. For B2B software, $40-$100/month works well.
principles.quote: $9/month lets you get lazy. $99/month doesn't let you hide.
